description: Quiral Labs: solo developer from Campina Grande, Brazil, building a tool to compare lunar landing sites by Sun and Earth visibility.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the lunar south pole. It shows, hour by hour, when the Sun is up for power and when Earth is in view for a direct radio link, over the real terrain horizon of each site.

- Sun and Earth positions come from NASA's SPICE ephemerides.
- The terrain comes from LRO's LOLA elevation model.
- Comparison: you can compare up to three sites.
- Any point: you can click any point on a 3D map and get results in under a second.

Our results match JPL Horizons to within 0.005° and NASA's PGDA illumination maps to within 1.5 percentage points on average.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, and Earth wobbles above and below it. A hill 10 km away can decide whether a lander has power or can talk to Earth, so flat-horizon estimates are not enough. Our tool builds the real 360° horizon of each site from NASA's LOLA terrain (including the Moon's curvature), tracks the Sun and Earth every hour from November 2026 to December 2028, and reports what a planner needs: how much of the Sun's disk is visible, whether Earth is in view, when the next sunset or Earthset comes, and how long the longest night lasts.

You can pick one of 10 candidate sites, search a crater name, type coordinates or click the 3D map. You can compare up to three sites for the next 30 days from any date. A month-by-month strip shows the share of hours with Sun, with Earth and with both for every month, so if a launch slips you see which month still works: at Malapert Massif, Sun and Earth together go from 37% of hours in April 2028 to 80% in October 2028. For students and the public, a four-step tour, "Why the south pole is hard", explains the physics with "Show me" buttons that set the app to the case that proves each point.

WHAT WE LEARNED

More sunlight does not always mean a better site. For a landing on 14 November 2026, Shackleton Rim is sunlit 87% of the time overall but has only 13 days with both Sun and Earth in the next 30 days. Malapert Massif has 22 days with both, because Earth stays in view much longer. The Shackleton crater floor, only about 10 km from the rim, gets 0% Sun and 0% Earth in two years: a permanently shadowed region where water ice may exist.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain: the LRO LOLA polar elevation model (120 m per pixel) is used to cast 720 rays from each site, up to 150 km. The highest terrain angle in each direction is the horizon.

2. Sun and Earth: NASA/NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) give their direction from the site every hour.

3. Visibility: we compare the Sun and Earth with the horizon (fraction of the Sun's disk above it; whether Earth's center is above it).

4. Browser: a static web app (Svelte, D3, three.js). For custom points it repeats the same calculation in the browser on a 240 m version of the terrain.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.005° (automated tests). The sunlit share matches NASA's PGDA average illumination maps within 1.5 percentage points on average across the 10 sites. The horizon code is tested on two cases with exact answers (a smooth sphere and a wall of known height). Limits are stated in the app: 120 m terrain resolution (240 m for custom points), no atmosphere or refraction, and Earth counts as visible when its center is above the horizon.

WHY IT MATTERS

Artemis missions plan to land near the south pole. A planner can use this tool to choose a landing date with the most days of both power and a direct link, see the exact hour when the Sun or Earth will disappear, and check any spot in seconds without installing software.

CODE

https://github.com/marcelin1555/lunar-landing-site-navigator

USE OF AI

We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) for research, discussing the architecture, generating and reviewing code, and helping translate this written submission from Portuguese to English. The author made all design decisions, checked the data and results against NASA references (JPL Horizons and PGDA maps), and reviewed the final work. No images, video or audio in this project were generated by AI: the demo is a screen recording of the real app.
